content: In resource-limited settings, the Guideline Development Group (GDG) emphasized that equity and access could influence the selection and type of tuberculosis (TB) diagnostic tests used. They strongly recommended two tests as equivalent options, noting their similar advantages and disadvantages. However, in 2011, the GDG concluded that the sensitivity and specificity of interferon-gamma release assays (IGRAs) for detecting active TB in individuals suspected of having TB were suboptimal, with low-quality evidence. They advised against using these tests as replacements for conventional microbiological methods for diagnosing pulmonary and extrapulmonary TB. Additionally, the GDG stated that current evidence did not support the use of IGRAs or the tuberculin skin test (TST) as part of the diagnostic work-up for adults suspected of active TB, regardless of HIV status. This recommendation prioritized avoiding unnecessary treatment due to the high rate of false-positive results associated with the low specificity of IGRAs and TST in these settings. The current recommendations are based on evaluations of all classes of TB infection diagnostic tests included in the respective assessments. However, the findings cannot be generalized to other brand-specific tests, and any new technologies in the same class must undergo specific evaluation by the World Health Organization (WHO) to determine their eligibility for procurement as in vitro diagnostics for TB. Updated policies are incorporated into the WHO TB Knowledge Sharing Platform, an online resource for global TB policies and related products. The Global TB Report collects and reports data on TB infection tests used by member countries, including WHO-recommended tests, as direct indicators of guideline uptake. Data on TB patient contact investigations and preventive treatment are also included as indirect indicators of guideline implementation. TB infection is characterized by a persistent immune response to Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) antigens without clinical evidence of active disease. Approximately one-quarter of the global population is estimated to be infected with Mtb. Testing for TB infection helps identify individuals who would benefit most from TB preventive treatment (TPT). However, there is no gold-standard test for diagnosing TB infection. The two currently available test types—TST and IGRAs—are indirect tests that rely on immune sensitization. A positive result from either test does not reliably predict the risk of progression to active disease. In 2011, WHO issued recommendations on the use of IGRAs for diagnosing TB infection, including the blood-based QIAGEN QuantiFERON®-TB Gold (QFT-G), QuantiFERON-TB Gold In-Tube (QFT-GIT), and Oxford Immunotec T-SPOT®.TB (T-SPOT) assays. In 2018, WHO updated its recommendations, allowing the use of either TST or IGRAs (or both) for testing TB infection in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). The TST is a widely used point-of-care test involving intradermal injection of purified protein derivative (PPD), which elicits a delayed-type hypersensitivity response, causing induration at the injection site within 48–72 hours. However, the TST's interpretation can be influenced by factors such as prior Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccination or infection with nontuberculous mycobacteria (NTM), necessitating population-specific cut-offs for interpretation. Unlike the TST, IGRAs are unaffected by prior BCG vaccination or most NTM infections. However, IGRAs are more expensive, require specialized facilities, and need trained personnel, making the TST the most commonly used test globally. Recent global shortages of PPD have highlighted the need for alternative tests. Newer Mtb antigen-based skin tests (TBSTs) have been developed, combining the simplicity of skin-test platforms with the specificity of IGRAs. These include Cy-Tb (Serum Institute of India), Diaskintest® (Generium, Russian Federation), and C-TST (formerly ESAT-6-CFP-10 test, Anhui Zhifei Longcom, China). These tests involve intradermal injection of antigens and are read as induration in millimeters after 48–72 hours, similar to the TST. Emerging evidence suggests that TBSTs may have comparable specificity to IGRAs and provide more reliable results in children, adolescents, and people living with HIV (PLHIV) than the TST. However, this evidence has not been systematically reviewed. WHO's assessment process for TB diagnostics now focuses on evaluating classes of technologies rather than specific products. Key factors guiding implementation include diagnostic accuracy, epidemiological and geographical settings, operational aspects (e.g., turnaround times, infrastructure), economic considerations, and qualitative aspects such as acceptability and equity. The TBST class is defined as in vivo skin tests using Mtb-specific antigens (ESAT-6 and CFP-10). In 2021, WHO commissioned a systematic review of published and unpublished data on this new class of tests, including diagnostic accuracy, safety, economic aspects, and qualitative evidence on feasibility and acceptability. The GDG convened in early 2022 to review the findings and make recommendations on TBSTs. The evaluated technologies included Cy-Tb, Diaskintest, and C-TST. The recommendations are based on data from these tests and cannot be extrapolated to other brand-specific tests. Any new in-class technologies will require specific evaluation by WHO. The updated policy is available on the WHO TB Knowledge Sharing Platform. The GDG concluded that the diagnostic accuracy of TBSTs is similar to IGRAs and superior to the TST. However, concerns were raised about the quality of evidence and the lack of longitudinal studies assessing the impact on TB outcomes. Safety concerns were not identified, but regulatory approval for individual products is essential before their introduction. Limited data on cost and cost-effectiveness suggest that TBSTs could be cost-saving compared to TST and IGRAs in some settings, such as Brazil and South Africa. Qualitative evidence indicates that TBSTs are likely to improve health equity by providing a more accurate, low-cost test for resource-limited settings where the TST is already in use. TBSTs are recommended for use in PLHIV, children and adolescents under 18 years, and individuals vaccinated with BCG. Testing for TB infection is not a prerequisite for initiating TPT in children under five years who are household contacts of people with active TB, but it increases certainty about the benefits of TPT. All three evaluated TBSTs—Cy-Tb, Diaskintest, and C-TST—are recommended for detecting TB infection.
